bibliographic.title: Whistleblowing in financial practice: a review of processes and impacts
bibliographic.citation_apa: Al-Thani, N., & Wright, S. (2026). Whistleblowing in financial practice: a review of processes and impacts. Frontiers in Sociology, 11, 1725253. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsoc.2026.1725253

methodology.method_family: theory-informed narrative synthesis within integrative review design
methodology.study_design: integrative review with five-theory analytic framework (moral judgement, power dependence, expectancy, institutional, and network governance)
methodology.sample_description: publications from 2000 to 2025 selected using relevance-based selection
methodology.technology_context: whistleblowing processes, outcomes, and cross-national policy effectiveness in financial services; brief mention of blockchain and generative AI as prospective reporting channels

eligibility.exclusion_reason: The article is a critical integrative review of whistleblowing processes and impacts in financial services. Generative AI appears only as a brief prospective mention for identifying and reporting wrongdoing, not as the object of conversational or LLM governance analysis.
eligibility.decision_rationale: Although the text addresses governance, accountability, compliance, oversight, and regulated financial contexts, the central research object is whistleblowing behavior and protection policy, not governance of conversational or LLM-based systems. Keyword overlap with the review scope does not constitute substantive evidence on conversational AI governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: The mismatch between the article's central topic and the review scope is clear from the abstract, objectives, and the limited generative AI mention.

appraisal.notes: Appraisal reflects the whistleblowing review itself. Relevance-based selection from 2000 to 2025 is described, but the provided text does not report search strategy detail, inclusion counts, or PRISMA-style flow. Limitations are not visible in the excerpt.

cerqual.explanation: The study appears internally coherent as an integrative whistleblowing review, but its relevance to conversational governance in LLM-based regulated systems is very low because LLM content is peripheral and conversational systems are not addressed.

coding.theme: Whistleblowing processes and outcomes in financial practice
coding.subtheme: Cross-national protection, enforcement, and organizational-cultural determinants of disclosure

synthesis.main_claim: Whistleblower outcomes in financial services are shaped by negotiations among individual moral characteristics, organizational power dynamics, institutional barriers, and regulatory networks, with stronger protection under regimes such as Sarbanes-Oxley, Dodd-Frank, and the EU directive.
synthesis.contribution: Provides a multi-level conceptual framework integrating five theoretical lenses to explain whistleblowing processes, outcomes, and cross-national policy effectiveness in financial services.
synthesis.use_in_review: Exclude from central or supporting evidence on conversational governance in LLM systems; at most peripheral contextual background on accountability and compliance in regulated finance, not on LLM deployment governance.

evidence.claim: Central topic is whistleblowing in financial practice, not LLM or conversational system governance.
evidence.excerpt: This critical review provides an integrative summary of the literature to develop a multi-theoretical model describing whistleblowing processes, outcomes, and cross-national policy effectiveness within financial services.

evidence.claim: Study uses an integrative review with theory-informed narrative synthesis.
evidence.excerpt: The review employs a theory-informed narrative synthesis within an integrative review design, analyzing publications from 2000 to 2025 using relevance-based selection

evidence.claim: Analytic framework combines five theories into a multi-level conceptual framework.
evidence.excerpt: a five-theory analytic framework (moral judgement, power dependence, expectancy, institutional, and network governance). Evidence was synthesized within each theoretical lens and then integrated to construct a multi-level conceptual framework.
The financial services sector is widely recognized as carrying significant fraud risk

evidence.claim: Governance and accountability terms refer to whistleblowing and public-interest disclosure, not AI governance.
evidence.excerpt: Insofar as whistleblowing ensures accountability and promotes the public interest regarding the activities of government

evidence.claim: Generative AI is only briefly mentioned as a prospective whistleblowing aid, not studied as a governed conversational system.
evidence.excerpt: Moreover, it has been suggested that generative AI could help employees identify wrongdoing and report it (Dimitrios, 2019).

evidence.claim: Authors' own generative AI use was limited to manuscript preparation, not the study subject.
evidence.excerpt: Generative AI statement The author(s) declared that generative AI was used in the creation of this manuscript. Language editing and clarity.

evidence.claim: No conversational AI, chatbot, agent, RAG, or LLM governance mechanisms are addressed in the provided text.
evidence.excerpt: KEYWORDS financial accountability, fraud deterrence, organizational culture, regulatory compliance, whistleblower protection, whistleblowing
